questions.explanation: includes reports whether a value is present using same-value matching, so finding 2693 yields true. indexOf would return the position instead of a boolean. The printed value is true, while the alternatives come from assuming includes uses strict reference only for objects, returning the found element and returning an index-style position.
questions.hint: includes returns a boolean, not a position.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — length.

options.misconception: Counting push as adding two slots
Counting before the push is applied

questions.explanation: push appends one element, so the list grows from 3 to 4 entries. The length property always counts elements, not the highest index. The printed value is 4, while the alternatives come from counting before the push is applied, counting push as adding two slots and using a zero-based length.
questions.hint: push adds exactly one element to the end of an array.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — slice.
questions.explanation: slice takes elements from index 1 up to but not including index 3, which is two elements. The end boundary is exclusive, a common source of off-by-one confusion. Carrying the operation through gives 2; common slips include treating the slice end index as included and treating the start index as the end.
questions.hint: The second argument of slice is not part of the result.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — splice.

options.misconception: Reporting the count of removed items instead
Removing one item instead of two
Assuming splice leaves the array unchanged

questions.explanation: splice removes two elements starting at index 1 and returns them, leaving 3 elements. Unlike slice, splice changes the original array in place. The printed value is 3, while the alternatives come from assuming splice leaves the array unchanged, reporting the count of removed items instead and removing one item instead of two.
questions.hint: splice is destructive: the original array shrinks by the removed count.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — map.

options.misconception: Assuming map returns the original element

questions.explanation: map applies the doubling callback to every element and returns a new array, so the first output is 2697 times two, or 5394. The source array is not changed. The printed value is 5394, while the alternatives come from assuming map returns the original element, adding instead of multiplying and dividing rather than doubling.
questions.hint: map builds a new array from each callback result.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — filter.
questions.explanation: filter keeps only values strictly greater than 74; exactly 2 of the three entries qualify. Elements equal to the threshold are rejected by the strict comparison. Carrying the operation through gives 2; common slips include assuming every element passes the test and counting rejected items instead of kept ones.
questions.hint: Check each element against the strict greater-than test.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — reduce.
questions.explanation: reduce folds every element into the accumulator starting from zero, producing the sum 2720. The initial value is the seed, not an extra element. The printed value is 2720, while the alternatives come from taking only the first element, omitting the last element and starting the accumulator at one.
questions.hint: The accumulator starts at the supplied initial value.
